## fal pricing in short

fal prices two products on one page with rate sheets in place of plans: GPU hours for serverless compute across six SKUs, and model APIs billed per output unit across video, image, audio and 3D. The "Units per $1" column turns seconds, tokens, images, megapixels, characters, generations and credits into one number a buyer compares directly.

...

- 1 The model stated in the hero"fal adapts to your usage, ensuring you only pay for the computing power you consume." The hero names usage pricing before any table, so the reader arrives at the rate sheets knowing there is no plan to choose.
- 2 Proof before the first price A logo strip with SUNO, World Labs, Adobe, Shopify, KREA and HeyGen sits above "Trusted by over 2,500,000 developers and leading companies." Placing scale and named customers ahead of the rate sheet frames every price that follows.
- 3 Anchor price in the copy"as low as $2.49/hr for H100" appears in the section intro before the table, giving scanners a benchmark number for the platform's best-known GPU.
- 4 List and floor, side by side Each GPU carries a list price and an "As low as" rate, with B300 running from $12.99/h to $5.99/h. Paired with the "Contact Sales" button under the table, the floor points to rates that move with commitment or volume, set in a conversation.
- 5 A new GB200 rung GB200 at 192 GB lists at $9.99/h with a $5.89/h floor, slotting between B300 and B200. Adding a SKU as a row keeps the rate card a single ladder that grows with the fleet.
- 6 Two paths at every table"Start Building" and "Contact Sales" appear under the GPU, video and image tables. A usage-priced product lets a developer start at any rate, and the paired button opens the conversation where negotiated rates live.
- 7 Units per $1 normalization Converting $0.05 and $0.015 per second into "20 seconds" and "66.67 seconds" per dollar makes models with different prices and units directly comparable, which is the buying question a developer brings.
- 8 Endpoint IDs on every row Each model name carries its API path, such as "minimax/h3-max/reference-to-video", so a price on the page maps one-to-one to the endpoint a developer calls and is billed for.
- 9 Tokens as a video unit Seedance 2 prices at $0.014 per 1000 tokens, giving 71.43 units per $1, beside rows billed in seconds. That points to fal passing through the unit each lab meters, while the shared column keeps the rows on one scale.
- 10 Assumptions printed with the math Footnotes state the 5-second 720p video and 1MP image basis and note that some models use GPU-based pricing. Showing the math behind a comparison column is what makes the comparison trustworthy.
- 11 Each intro names its unit"Audio models are billed per 1,000 characters or per second, depending on the model." The sentence before each table tells a buyer how to read it, so ElevenLabs at $0.1 per 1000 characters and ACE Step at $0.0002 per second sit side by side.
- 12 Credits passed through Tripo H3.1 rows bill in credits at $0.01, beside generations for Meshy 6 Preview at $0.8 and units for Sam 3 at $0.02. The 3D table carries three units under one intro, and the Units per $1 column turns each into a count per dollar.
- 13 A closing band with both paths"Build with the fastest inference platform on the planet." closes the rate sheets with Get Started and Contact Sales side by side, so a reader who scrolled every table lands on both next steps.
- 14 The footer is a model catalog The footer lists image models such as Seedream 5.0 and Flux 2, video models such as Kling 3.0 and Veo 3.1, and labs from Black Forest Labs to ByteDance. The page closes on the breadth of the catalog the rates apply to.

## How has fal's pricing changed?

1. October 26, 2026

GPU rates moved up across the fleet: H100 now runs as low as $2.49/h (from $1.89/h), B300 lists at $12.99/h with a $5.99/h floor, and a new GB200 row arrives at $9.99/h and $5.89/h. Model APIs grew from two short tables into four, with ten-row video and image tables, new Audio Models and 3D Models sections, endpoint IDs under each model, and the value column renamed "Units per $1". The enterprise contact form gave way to a logo strip reading "Trusted by over 2,500,000 developers and leading companies." and a closing "Build with the fastest inference platform on the planet." band.

## How does fal pricing work?

fal meters at two distances from the hardware. Serverless compute is raw capacity, a GPU-hour rate card with six SKUs from RTX PRO 6000 at $4.00/h list to B300 at $12.99/h list, each shown with its VRAM and an "As low as" rate, with H100 at $2.49/h. Model APIs are priced on outcomes, per output unit, and the unit follows the modality: seconds for H3 Max and Kling video, 1000 tokens for Seedance 2, images and megapixels for Nano Banana and FLUX.1 [schnell], 1000 characters or seconds for audio, and units, generations or credits for 3D. Output pricing fits generative media because customers think in clips, images and voice lines, and the "Units per $1" column, 20 seconds of H3 Max Reference to Video, 333.33 megapixels of FLUX.1 [schnell], 5,000 seconds of ACE Step audio, puts every unit on one scale.

Under the hood, the two rate sheets reveal two billing engines. GPU hours are a classic rate table with a list price and a floor, and the "As low as" column, paired with "Contact Sales", points to negotiated rates tied to volume or commitment, with the spread running from $5.99/h against $12.99/h on B300 to $2.49/h against $4.50/h on H100. Model APIs are output metering with pass-through economics: each endpoint carries its own rate in the unit its lab meters, and the footnotes show the math, an average video of 5 seconds at 720p, images normalized to 1MP with "Higher resolutions will be priced proportionally", and a note that some models "may use GPU-based pricing depending on architecture". Worth borrowing: when a catalog spans many units, a normalized value column with its assumptions printed underneath gives the buyer one comparison to make.

results.title: Fal Cuts Prices on H3 Max Video Models — AIVIDEO.NEWS
highlights:
# Fal Cuts Prices on H3 Max Video Models

Fal is temporarily halving the cost of its H3 Max and H3 Max Turbo video generation models, making the pair cheaper to run through the end of September.

AI Video Newsroom · Sep 16, 2026, 10:12 PM

Fal has rolled out a limited-time discount on two of its video generation offerings, H3 Max and H3 Max Turbo, cutting prices in half through September 30. During the promotional window, H3 Max will run at $0.04 per second of generated video at 768p resolution, while the faster H3 Max Turbo variant drops to $0.02 per second at the same resolution. The announcement frames the two models as among the quickest high-end video generators currently available, positioning the price cut as a way to get more creators and developers testing them before the discount expires. Fal did not specify what happens to pricing once the promotional period ends, so users looking to take advantage of the lower rates have a defined but short window to do so. Discounted pricing on frontier-tier generation tools has become a common tactic among AI video platforms competing for developer attention, and this move fits that pattern by lowering the barrier to experimenting with Fal's faster models. With H3 Max Turbo already positioned as the speed-optimized option, the added discount makes it one of the cheaper ways to access rapid, high-quality video generation for the next several weeks. For teams evaluating video generation infrastructure, the temporary rate cut offers a chance to benchmark output quality and speed against other providers without committing to full price. Whether the discount is extended or made permanent has not been addressed in Fal's announcement.

results.title: MiniMax H3 Max Turbo Version Released One Week Later, 2.5x Faster and Half the Price | KuCoin
highlights:
Release Time: 2026/09/03 03:24:03

On-chain news from ChainThink reveals that Fal launched the Turbo version of MiniMax H3 Max just one week after its initial release. The updated model is 2.5 times faster and reduces costs by half, with a standard price of $0.04 per second, down from $0.08. During the launch, the price drops to $0.01 per second, making the cost of one minute of video generation approximately $0.60. Internal testing shows the Turbo version retains 97% of the original’s quality while enhancing speed and affordability.

ChainThink reports that on September 3, according to an announcement by fal, the AI inference platform fal launched its Turbo version just one week after the release of MiniMax H3 Max, reducing generation latency by approximately 2.5 times and halving the price.

The Turbo version is post-trained on MiniMax H3 and optimized for the fal inference system. In official tests with 5-second, 768p videos, generation latency decreased from 3.49 seconds on H3 Max to 1.40 seconds.

In terms of quality, Fal's self-tested Turbo version achieves 97% of the original H3 Max, with prompt understanding, aesthetics, and overall quality largely preserved, remaining superior to the original MiniMax H3 and other tested models.

In terms of pricing, Turbo is normally $0.04 per second, which is only half the regular price of H3 Max ($0.08 per second). During the launch promotion, it is $0.01 per second, costing approximately $0.60 to generate a 1-minute video.

results.title: What Is fal? The Platform Behind AI Video's Launches
highlights:
fal is a company, not a model, a serverless cloud infrastructure platform that lets developers and creators access hundreds of AI image, video, audio, and 3D generation models through a single API, without needing to own, rent, or manage their own GPU hardware. When someone requests a generation, fal allocates the necessary compute, runs the model, streams the result back in real time, then releases those resources once the job is done. That's the entire value proposition: renting AI compute by the generation rather than by the hour, with none of the infrastructure headache.

...

fal's growth has been fast even by AI-industry standards. The company's valuation moved from roughly $1.5 billion in mid-2025 to $4.5 billion by December 2025, in a round led by Sequoia with participation from Nvidia's investment arm and Google's AI Futures Fund, and by early 2026 the company was reportedly in talks for a raise valuing it near $8 billion.

results.title: Earning Rate Changes: September 12 - SaladCloud Blog
results.author: Jared Carpenter
highlights:
# Earning Rate Changes: September 12

Salad earning rates change September 12, 2026: RTX 5090 and 4090 rates go up, 15 GPU classes come down at higher priority tiers, CPU payouts rise.

Jared Carpenter

Product Update SaladApp Fri Sep 04 2026

GPU prices will change on September 12th, 00:00 UTC. Before you worry, these changes include increased earnings for highly demanded GPUs, and almost all decreases are limited to specific priority tiers. See the chart below if you want to check what your future earning situation will look like. Keep reading for more context as to why we're altering our prices again.

If you're running a 5090 or a 4090, your rates are going up at High, Medium, and Low priority, since demand for those cards keeps outrunning what the network can supply. Fifteen other GPU classes are coming down, mostly at those same three tiers, while Lowest priority stays where it is on everything except the RTX 5080. CPU-only workloads are getting a raise too, covered below. And if your card isn't in the chart at all, nothing about your earnings is changing.

## Why prices are changing again Copy Anchor Link

For once, some of these changes are increases. Customer demand for the 5090 and 4090 has been outrunning what the network can supply for months now, so on September 12th those two classes get more expensive for customers, and your earning rates on them go up right along with it.

The rest of the changes are decreases across the higher priority tiers. Our lowest priority prices are already highly competitive with the market, so those aren't changing (the RTX 5080 being the one exception), but our higher tiers were overpriced, which discouraged customers from paying more for your GPUs. Needless to say, if our customers can get the same or comparable GPU resources elsewhere, at higher reliability, and cheaper than our higher priority prices, they can and will do so.

While we can't guarantee that this will lead to 100% uptime for everyone who owns the affected GPUs, we expect utilization and priority rates to both increase, leading to more Salad Balance heading into Chefs' pockets.

Payouts for CPU-only workloads are going from $0.0035 to $0.004 per hour per vCPU, which works out to a bit over 14% more for the exact same work.
